strengths: The core idea—using Laplace approximation to turn a single trained reference model into a BNN so that both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty can be captured for conditional MIA—is well-motivated and clearly distinguishes itself from quantile regression (QMIA) and multi-reference-model approaches (LiRA, Attack-R, RMIA).

The toy 1D regression example (Figure 1) is a clear and convincing illustration of why quantile regression underestimates variance in low-density regions while a BNN does not, grounding the main motivation of the paper.

Theoretical results (Propositions 4.1 and 4.2) formalize the intuition that conditional attacks are provably more powerful than marginal attacks under Gaussian score assumptions, filling a gap that prior empirical work left unaddressed.

Extensive experiments across five datasets (two tabular, three image, including ImageNet) and multiple baselines show that BMIA achieves higher TPR at very low FPR while using only 1 reference model versus 2/4/8 for competitors, with substantial wall-clock/GPU-time savings (e.g., ~1/8 the cost of LiRA n=8 on CIFAR-10 with a 64% relative TPR gain at 1% FPR).

Thorough ablations covering sample size sensitivity, Hessian factorization choice (KFAC vs diagonal vs full), architecture mismatch robustness, OOD non-member queries (CINIC-10), and predictive-distribution approximation choices (MC vs linearized), which support reproducibility and give practical guidance.
Reasonably detailed appendix with training/implementation details (data splits, hyperparameters, library used) aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claim that BMIA's Laplace-based estimate is a more faithful conditional distribution than QMIA's quantile regression is argued mainly via a low-dimensional toy example and general BNN uncertainty-decomposition arguments (Eq. 10); there is no direct theoretical or empirical bound quantifying the bias reduction of the last-layer Laplace approximation specifically for high-dimensional deep classifiers used in the main experiments.

The method treats only the last-layer weights probabilistically for computational efficiency, which may substantially underestimate epistemic uncertainty coming from the rest of the network; this approximation gap is not analyzed quantitatively, and its effect on attack fidelity vs. a full-network Laplace or true multi-model oracle (LiRA) is only shown indirectly through TPR numbers rather than a direct comparison of estimated vs. true conditional distributions.

The Gaussian assumption underlying both the hinge score and the reliance on the Student's t-test (Algorithm 1) is inherited from prior work and not independently validated in this paper (e.g., no goodness-of-fit checks across datasets/architectures), despite being central to both the algorithm and the theoretical propositions.

The magnitude of improvement over well-established SOTA baselines (e.g., 64% relative TPR gain over LiRA with n=8 using only n=1) is striking and could benefit from more scrutiny/discussion of why such large gaps arise (e.g., are baseline reference models trained under favorable-to-BMIA settings, sample-size effects, or hyperparameter tuning asymmetries between methods) to preempt concerns about fair comparison.

The efficiency comparison partly hinges on QMIA's reported hyperparameter-tuning cost being very large (e.g., 306 GPU-min on CIFAR-10); it is unclear whether this reflects an inherent limitation of QMIA or an artifact of the specific tuning protocol used, which affects the strength of the efficiency claim.

The Limitations section is brief and does not discuss potential weaknesses such as reliance on an accurate/representative population distribution π for sampling the reference dataset, dependence on last-layer approximation quality across architectures, or scenarios where the Gaussian score assumption might fail (e.g., non-classification tasks, highly asymmetric or multimodal score distributions).

strengths: The core idea of using Laplace-approximated BNNs to obtain both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty from a single reference model is a reasonable and potentially useful alternative to QMIA and multi-reference-model attacks (LiRA/Attack-R/RMIA), and is well motivated by the toy regression illustration in Fig.1 showing QR's failure to widen intervals in low-density regions.

The paper provides a theoretical treatment (Propositions 4.1, 4.2) attempting to explain formally why conditional/instance-wise attacks outperform marginal attacks, which prior empirical papers largely lacked.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation across five datasets (two tabular, three image, including ImageNet) and multiple baselines (Attack-P, Attack-R, LiRA, QMIA, RMIA) with reported computational cost, plus several useful ablations: sample size vs. TPR/inference time, Hessian factorization choice (KFAC vs diagonal vs full), reference/target architecture mismatch, and robustness to OOD non-members (CINIC-10).

Efficiency claims are well supported qualitatively: BMIA only requires one reference model and the additional Laplace fitting/inference overhead is shown to be small relative to training cost (Fig. 3c, Table 1 timings).
weaknesses: There is a serious and unexplained numerical inconsistency between the abstract and the main results: the abstract states BMIA achieves 37.5% TPR at 1% FPR on CIFAR-10 with a 64% improvement over LiRA, but Table 1 reports only 8.87% TPR at 1% FPR for BMIA on CIFAR-10 (with LiRA n=8 at 8.32%, an improvement of only ~7%, not 64%). This kind of large discrepancy between headline claims and the actual reported table casts doubt on the reliability/consistency of the reported numbers throughout the paper and is not addressed anywhere in the text.

The proof of Proposition 4.2 chains several inequalities (Jensen's inequality applied to a convex Φ, plus 'variance decomposition inequality' applied to a term that includes Φ^{-1}(α) which can be negative for small α) without carefully verifying that the sign of the multiplied quantities preserves the inequality direction; the argument is stated as if it holds generally but the chain is only rigorously valid for restricted parameter regimes (e.g., TPR(z) < 0.5 is assumed but the sign behavior of µS-µD+Φ^{-1}(α)σD(z) under multiplication is not discussed), reducing confidence in the generality of the claimed result.

BMIA only performs Bayesian treatment on the last layer (last-layer Laplace), which is a strong approximation that limits how much of the network's true epistemic uncertainty is captured; this design choice is described as being for efficiency but its impact on the quality/completeness of the uncertainty estimate relative to full-network Bayesian treatment is not rigorously analyzed beyond an ablation on Hessian factorization (which is a separate axis).

No variance/confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics are reported for the main comparison in Table 1, making it hard to judge whether the reported gains over LiRA/RMIA (especially at very low FPRs such as 0.1%, where TPR estimates are inherently high-variance due to few positive predictions) are statistically meaningful rather than noise.

The experimental protocol splits data as 20% target-train/20% target-test/40% population (further halved for reference-model training)/20% held out for QMIA and RMIA; it is unclear whether this exact split is equally favorable to all baselines, particularly since reference models for competing multi-model methods are trained on smaller subsets of the population while BMIA's single reference model may see a comparably sized or different subset — a more detailed accounting of data budget per method would strengthen fairness claims.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with the dual-use nature of improved, cheaper MIAs (e.g., how a highly efficient one-reference-model attack lowers the barrier for real-world privacy attacks, or how the technique could inform defenses), which is a missed opportunity given the paper explicitly aims to make MIAs more practical/efficient.

The improvement over quantile regression (QMIA) is argued primarily via a single one-dimensional toy example (Fig. 1) and a single qualitative case study (Fig. 2) rather than a more systematic quantitative study isolating the epistemic-uncertainty benefit from other confounding factors (e.g., different score approximations, sampling strategies).

strengths: The core idea—reusing Laplace approximation to convert a single trained reference model into a BNN, thereby obtaining both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty for the conditional score distribution—is a clean and reasonably novel adaptation of existing Bayesian deep learning tools to the MIA setting, directly targeting the known weakness of QMIA (failure to capture epistemic uncertainty in low-density regions).

The paper provides a theoretical grounding (Propositions 4.1 and 4.2) for why conditional attacks are more powerful than marginal attacks under a Gaussian-score assumption, going beyond prior empirical claims in Carlini et al. and Ye et al.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five datasets (two tabular, three image, including ImageNet) and multiple strong baselines (Attack-P/R, LiRA, QMIA, RMIA) with consistent gains in TPR at low FPR alongside large computational savings (single reference model vs. 2/4/8 shadow models or an expensive quantile-regression model).

Useful ablations: effect of sample size and inference time (parallelizable sampling costs little extra time), sensitivity to Hessian factorization (KFAC vs diagonal vs full), choice of predictive-distribution approximation (MC vs linearized), and hyperparameter tuning strategy for the prior variance — these support the practical reproducibility of the method.
Additional robustness studies (mismatched target/reference architectures, OOD non-members from CINIC-10) strengthen the practical relevance of the approach beyond the standard benchmark setting.
weaknesses: There appears to be a numerical inconsistency between the abstract's headline claim ("37.5% TPR at 1% FPR, a 64% improvement over LiRA on CIFAR-10") and Table 1, where the CIFAR-10 TPR@1% for BMIA is 8.87 (not 37.5) and the closest matching 64%-type comparison (35.75 vs 23.20, ~54% relative gain) actually corresponds to CIFAR-100, not CIFAR-10. This discrepancy is not explained anywhere in the text and undermines confidence in the reported headline numbers.

The method only treats the last-layer weights probabilistically (for efficiency), which is a substantial approximation of the full BNN framework motivating the paper; the extent to which this restricted treatment still captures meaningful epistemic uncertainty from earlier, more expressive layers (where much of the memorization is believed to occur) is not rigorously justified, only empirically spot-checked via a small Hessian-approximation ablation.

The theoretical results (Propositions 4.1/4.2) rely on fairly strong and somewhat informally justified assumptions: independence between mean/variance terms across z, a Gaussian score assumption for hinge scores, and a chain of Jensen/variance-decomposition inequalities whose direction and tightness are not carefully discussed or empirically validated beyond the toy illustrative example in Figure 1/2.

No variance/error bars or repeated-trial statistics are reported for the main results in Table 1 (single train/test split per dataset), making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements, especially at very low FPR where TPR estimates can be noisy.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with the dual-use nature of MIA research (e.g., how BMIA's efficiency could lower the barrier for real-world privacy attacks) despite this being directly relevant to a paper about attack methodology.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important practical problem: the prohibitive computational cost of training many reference/shadow models for conditional MIAs (e.g., LiRA, Attack-R), and proposes a principled single-model alternative via Laplace approximation.

Solid theoretical contribution: formal variance decomposition (Proposition 3.1) into intra-model and inter-model variance components, plus a theorem (3.2) proving that increasing posterior samples M monotonically increases statistical power; also provides a novel formal explanation (Appendix B) for why conditional attacks outperform marginal attacks, filling a gap in prior literature.

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation across 10 datasets spanning three modalities (image, text, tabular) and multiple architectures (ResNet, DenseNet, BERT, DistilBERT, MLP), compared against five strong baselines (Attack-P, Attack-R, LiRA, QMIA, RMIA).

Strong efficiency-effectiveness tradeoff demonstrated: BMIA with a single reference model matches or exceeds multi-reference baselines (n=8) while using roughly 1/8 the training compute, which is a meaningful practical contribution.

Thorough ablation and robustness studies: sample size sensitivity, Hessian factorization choice (KFAC vs diagonal vs full), alternative Bayesian inference methods (SWAG, MC Dropout, ensembles), architecture mismatch, distribution shift in reference data, and OOD query robustness.

Good supplementary diagnostics (Appendix F) empirically validating the Gaussian assumption underlying the t-test via QQ-plots and t-statistic distributions, and a clear discussion of computational complexity/scalability of the last-layer Laplace approach (Appendix G.2).
weaknesses: The central conceptual claim—that posterior sampling from a single reference model via Laplace approximation can substitute for the variance that would arise from retraining on many resampled datasets—is only rigorously justified for linear/Gaussian models (Appendix A.3); for deep networks this equivalence is heuristic, and the last-layer-only LA further limits how much of the true epistemic uncertainty is captured, which could undermine the theoretical narrative's generality.

Some reported improvements over well-established strong baselines (e.g., BMIA achieving 35.75% vs LiRA n=8's 23.20% TPR@1%FPR on CIFAR-100, a >50% relative gain) are unusually large; more discussion/validation of baseline implementation fidelity (hyperparameters, shadow model training matching original papers) would strengthen confidence that comparisons are fully fair.

Direct single-reference-model comparisons (Ours n=1 vs. RMIA n=1) are only shown for CIFAR-10/100 (Table 2) rather than across all ten datasets, leaving efficiency-matched comparisons on tabular and text datasets less complete.

The Gaussian/parametric score assumption underlying the t-test may not hold in all settings (acknowledged in Appendix F.1 with a fallback calibration suggestion), but the main paper does not extensively validate this assumption across all evaluated datasets/architectures, only via limited diagnostics.
The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with the dual-use or ethical implications of releasing an efficient, higher-power MIA tool.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated practical problem: reducing the computational cost of conditional MIAs that traditionally require training many shadow/reference models (LiRA, Attack-R).

The core idea of using Laplace approximation posterior sampling on a single reference model to approximate the conditional score distribution is a reasonably novel and elegant repurposing of Bayesian deep learning tools for privacy auditing.

A formal variance-decomposition analysis (intra-model vs inter-model variance) is provided with proofs, offering a plausible theoretical account of why Bayesian sampling can improve statistical power, and this naturally motivates the multi-reference extension (MR-BMIA).

Experimental coverage is broad: two tabular, three image, and five text datasets, with numerous architectures, plus ablations on Hessian factorization (KFAC vs diagonal vs full), number of posterior samples, alternative Bayesian/ensemble inference methods, hyperparameter tuning strategies, and predictive-distribution approximations (MC vs LLN).

Robustness experiments are included for practically relevant threat-model variations: reference model trained on a different dataset, OOD non-member queries, and target/reference architecture mismatch.

Appendix provides useful diagnostics for the Gaussian score assumption (QQ-plots, t-statistic histograms) and an explicit complexity analysis explaining why last-layer Laplace scales well compared to full-Hessian approaches.
weaknesses: A central theoretical/practical tension is under-addressed: Proposition 3.1 shows the total score variance decomposes into intra-model and inter-model components, and the paper's own linear-regression interpretation (Appendix A.3) explicitly notes that single-reference posterior sampling does not remove the dataset-to-dataset fluctuation of the estimator center (i.e., inter-model variance/bias is not captured when K=1). Yet the main experimental comparisons (Table 1, Table 2, Table 6) use BMIA with K=1 and report large improvements over multi-reference baselines (LiRA/Attack-R/RMIA with n up to 8) that are specifically designed to estimate this inter-model variability. The paper does not clearly reconcile how ignoring a variance component the theory itself identifies as important yields such large gains, nor does it verify that the nominal FPRs used for the TPR@FPR comparisons are empirically well-calibrated for the K=1 variant.

The magnitude of the reported improvements is very large (e.g., 54% relative TPR improvement over LiRA n=8 at 1% FPR on CIFAR-100, and BMIA with 1 reference model beating 8-reference LiRA/RMIA across nearly every dataset), which is a surprising result given the design intuition behind shadow-model ensembles; this warrants more rigorous statistical validation (e.g., variance/confidence intervals across repeated experiments with different random reference datasets/seeds) beyond the single std-only ablation reported in Appendix Table 9 for one setting.

The empirical diagnostics for the Gaussian assumption underlying the t-test (Appendix F.1) are based on only a handful of arbitrarily/qualitatively selected query points and simple visual QQ-plots, rather than a systematic quantitative normality test (e.g., Shapiro-Wilk, Anderson-Darling) aggregated over many samples and datasets; this is a comparatively weak validation of a core modeling assumption that underlies the entire hypothesis-testing framework.

The method relies on last-layer Laplace approximation, meaning epistemic uncertainty from the majority of the network's parameters (the feature extractor/backbone) is not modeled at all; this restricts the claimed 'aleatoric + epistemic uncertainty' capture to only the last layer, which is a significant simplification not sufficiently discussed as a limitation in the main text.

Table 1's time comparisons for reference-model training do not fully account for the additional cost of Hessian construction/posterior fitting for BMIA in a way that is easy to compare apples-to-apples with baseline training times, and the inference-time analysis (Fig. 1c) is limited to CIFAR-10/100 only, leaving efficiency claims for text/tabular/ImageNet less substantiated at the inference stage.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with the dual-use nature of proposing a stronger, cheaper membership inference attack, nor with implications for practitioners relying on differential privacy or other defenses potentially being under- or over-estimated in effectiveness against this new attack.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important practical problem: state-of-the-art conditional MIAs (LiRA, Attack-R) require training many reference models, which is computationally prohibitive; BMIA achieves comparable or better attack power with a single reference model via Laplace approximation, yielding roughly 8x lower training cost than n=8 baselines.

Solid theoretical contribution: the paper formally explains, via a law-of-total-variance decomposition (Prop 3.1) and a t-test/Welch-Satterthwaite construction, why Bayesian sampling from a single reference model reduces intra-model variance and provably increases statistical power (Theorem 3.2). It also gives a novel argument (Prop B.1/B.2) for why conditional attacks generally outperform marginal ones, filling a gap not formally addressed in prior work (Carlini et al. 2022; Ye et al. 2022).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three modalities (2 tabular, 3 image, 5 text datasets) and multiple architectures, with consistent state-of-the-art TPR@low-FPR improvements over Attack-P/R, LiRA, RMIA, and QMIA at matched or lower computational cost (e.g., 54% TPR improvement over LiRA n=8 on CIFAR-100 with 1/8 the cost).

Extensive ablations and robustness checks: sample size vs. TPR, Hessian factorization choice (Diagonal vs KFAC vs Full), Bayesian inference method comparisons (SWAG, MC Dropout, ensembling methods), distribution-shifted reference data, OOD queries, and architecture mismatch between target and reference models — showing the method is robust in realistic, imperfect-knowledge settings.

Good treatment of assumptions and limitations: the appendix explicitly diagnoses the Gaussian assumption underlying the t-test (QQ-plots, t-statistic distributions) and discusses a calibration fallback (conformal p-values) for cases where the assumption fails, which is a responsible and often-overlooked addition.

The multi-reference extension (MR-BMIA) is a natural, theoretically motivated generalization that further improves performance when more compute is available, showing the framework scales gracefully rather than being a one-off trick.
weaknesses: The core theoretical results (Prop 3.1, Theorem 3.2) rely on treating scores/logits as jointly Gaussian and on variance decompositions that, while empirically supported for hinge scores in the appendix, are asymptotic/parametric approximations; the practical tightness of the derived test (e.g., validity of Welch-Satterthwaite dof approximation with correlated per-model samples) is not rigorously stress-tested beyond a few diagnostic plots on CIFAR.

The last-layer Laplace approximation only captures uncertainty in the final linear layer, ignoring epistemic uncertainty from the feature extractor; this could understate uncertainty for examples where representation-level overfitting occurs, and the paper does not empirically probe how much this restriction affects attack power relative to a full-network (or more layers) Laplace approximation.

Comparisons to multi-reference baselines fix small n (2,4,8) for LiRA/Attack-R/RMIA in the main table, which may understate their potential performance since these methods are known to keep improving with much larger n (as shown by the paper's own Table 3/7 using n up to 64/128); a more complete comparison at matched total training budget (not just matched n) would strengthen the efficiency claims.

Text and tabular dataset descriptions are relatively thin (e.g., architecture/training details for BERT/DistilBERT/MLP fine-tuning are deferred largely to accuracy tables), and some designs choices (e.g., prior precision tuning via marginal likelihood vs. validation-based tuning) are shown to make little difference only on CIFAR, not validated across all modalities.

The architecture-mismatch and cross-dataset robustness experiments (Figure 2) are conducted only on CIFAR-10/CINIC-10 and a limited set of vision architectures; it remains unclear how well BMIA's robustness claims transfer to text or tabular domains where reference/target mismatch could behave differently.
